Brachial Plexus Injury at Birth

birth trauma · upper and lower plexus · Moro, biceps and grasp

1Script2Urgent3Differential4Workup5Criteria6Severity7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Illness script
Bottom line
  • Absent grasp with preserved Moro and biceps reflexes, a clawed hand and same-side ptosis or miosis point to Klumpke palsy (C8-T1).
  • Moro and biceps decreased, grasp preserved: Erb-Duchenne palsy (C5-C6) (Erb palsy, waiter's tip palsy). Crepitus with biceps and grasp preserved favors a fracture.
  • Start protective positioning and gentle physical therapy. No improvement over 1 to 2 months needs specialist evaluation; consider repair for persistent deficits rather than simply reassuring.
What it is

Delivery-associated injury to the nerves supplying the arm and hand

Driver

Traction or compression may stretch, tear or avulse the involved nerves

Triggers

Shoulder dystocia, difficult extraction or a large infant (non-modifiable)

Maternal diabetes may contribute through a large infant (non-modifiable)

Chain

Lateral neck traction upper-trunk injury shoulder and elbow weakness

Upward arm traction lower-trunk injury intrinsic-hand weakness

Insights

Use the reflex pattern. Grasp tests the lower distribution; biceps and the upper-arm component of Moro distinguish the classic upper palsy.

Horner changes prognosis. Lower-root sympathetic involvement can cause ptosis and miosis and predicts a poorer outcome.

What the injury does, by levelMotor localization
ShoulderDeltoid and supraspinatus weakness leaves the arm adductedInfraspinatus weakness leaves it internally rotated
ElbowBiceps weakness impairs flexion and supinationThe forearm rests extended and pronated
Upper-trunk musclesBiceps, infraspinatus, wrist extensors, deltoid and supraspinatus
HandLumbricals, interossei and thenar/hypothenar muscles can be weakLoss of intrinsic muscle balance allows clawing
2Urgent risks
BreathingArm weakness with respiratory distress or reduced breath sounds on one side

If a phrenic injury may accompany the plexus injury, choose assess breathing urgently and support ventilation as needed.

Extensive injuryA flail arm, absent reflexes or a sensory deficit

If the entire plexus or cord may be involved, choose obtain urgent specialist assessment; cord signs require MRI.

3Differential
A weak arm at birth: reflexes by lesion
DiagnosisMoro / biceps / grasp, or central patternDecides it
Erb-Duchenne palsy (Erb palsy, waiter's tip palsy)Decreased / decreased / preservedAt birth; adducted, internally rotated arm; extended elbow, pronated forearm, flexed wrist; C5-C6Root extentUpper-plexus injury may include C7 as well as C5 and C6. The classic Erb pattern used here localizes to C5-C6; an extensive injury can involve more roots.
Klumpke palsyPreserved / preserved / absentAt birth; a clawed hand, sometimes Horner syndrome; C8-T1
Clavicle fracturePain-limited / preserved / preservedClavicular crepitus or irregularity; pain inhibits the Moro response
Humerus fracturePain-limited / preserved / preservedCrepitus or swelling in the upper arm
Total plexus palsyAbsent / absent / absentFlaccid arm; sensory loss and Horner suggest more extensive injury
Perinatal ischemic strokeUpper motor neuron signs may emergeUpper motor neuron signs rather than an isolated peripheral-nerve pattern
Perinatal asphyxiaPoor tone with altered alertnessAltered alertness, poor tone, feeding or breathing problems, seizures
4Workup
Clues that change the next step
CluePoints toNext best step
Moro and biceps reduced; grasp preservedUpper-trunk palsyAssess movement and follow recovery
Crepitus with biceps and grasp preservedA painful fractureObtain a radiograph at the tender site
Pyramidal signs after birth traumaPossible associated cord injuryMRI with urgent specialist assessment

Pause point. A reduced Moro reflex alone does not prove a nerve injury: a fracture can make the response painful. Grasp and biceps, plus the bony examination, separate the two.

5Diagnostic criteria
Clinical localization
FindingInterpretation
Waiter's-tip posture with biceps and Moro decreased, grasp intactClassic C5-C6 upper-trunk injury
Metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints extended, interphalangeal (IP) joints flexed; grasp absentClaw hand from lower C8-T1 injury
Ipsilateral ptosis and miosisHorner syndrome from sympathetic involvement; poorer prognosis
6Severity
Recovery and extent
FindingMeans
Early return of movementImprovement is expected in many stretch injuries; continue observation and therapy
Horner syndrome or persistent sensory lossGreater concern for severe root injury and a poor recovery
Flail arm and absent reflexesPossible total plexus injury; more extensive than isolated Erb or Klumpke palsy
7Treatment
1

Protectimmediately after birth injury

Protect the shoulder and position the arm; avoid excessive motion
2

Therapyduring early recovery

Usually supportive: gentle passive range of motion with physical therapy; begin daily joint motion from about 1 week
3

Specialistno improvement over 1 to 2 months, or a severe deficit

Refer for neurologic and orthopedic assessment of recovery and possible repair
4

Repairdeficits persist despite therapy

Consider nerve surgery, often assessed over 3 to 9 months; earlier referral is separate from the timing of repair
8Follow-up
Follow-up decisions
WhenDo
During the first weeksRecord return of shoulder movement, elbow flexion and grasp; prevent joint contractures
Motor recovery remains incompleteTrack shoulder, elbow and hand movement; apply the referral criteria in step 7
Persistent motor deficitMonitor limb growth and discuss reconstructive options with the team
Practice
  1. A newborn's right shoulder and elbow move normally, but the hand barely moves. Grasp is absent; Moro and biceps reflexes are symmetric. The wrist is extended and fingers clawed. Right ptosis and miosis; no crepitus → Lower brachial plexus (C8-T1) injury → Klumpke palsy
  2. 1-day-old girl, 4.6 kg, after shoulder dystocia; the left arm lies adducted and internally rotated with the elbow extended, forearm pronated and wrist flexed; left Moro and biceps reflexes absent; left grasp strong; no crepitus; pupils equal → Erb-Duchenne palsy → Physical therapy with gentle range of motion
  3. 2-day-old boy after shoulder dystocia, moves the right arm less; right Moro diminished and he cries when the arm is moved; biceps reflex and grasp present on both sides; crepitus midway between the sternal notch and the right shoulder → Clavicle fracture → Gentle handling and pain control
  4. 3-week-old girl with an Erb palsy from a shoulder dystocia delivery; she has begun to flex the elbow a little; no crepitus; radiographs of the clavicle and humerus are normal → Range-of-motion exercises with physical therapy → Upper brachial plexus (C5-C6) injury
  5. 7-month-old boy with a left upper brachial plexus injury from birth who has had physical therapy since the first weeks; he still has no elbow flexion or shoulder abduction on the left → Referral for surgical nerve repair → Upper brachial plexus (C5-C6) injury without recovery
  6. 3-day-old girl with weakness of the right arm after a difficult vaginal delivery → Ipsilateral ptosis and miosis → Horner syndrome from a T1 injury
Management and prognosis Gentle range-of-motion exercises with physical therapy to prevent contractures; most infants recover within months. Apply the specialist referral criteria in Treatment; persistent deficits may need surgical nerve repair. Horner syndrome marks a T1 injury and predicts a poorer outcome. A birth clavicle fracture generally heals with gentle handling and pain control.
Pearls Risk factors: macrosomia, shoulder dystocia and maternal diabetes · Traction on the head and neck during shoulder dystocia stretches the upper roots (Erb); traction on a raised arm, as in delivering the posterior arm, stretches C8-T1 (Klumpke) · An intact, symmetric Moro does not exclude a plexus injury, because Klumpke spares the shoulder; check the grasp
Pairs with Arm Injury in a Young Child: sorts pediatric arm and elbow injuries. Torticollis and Plagiocephaly in an Infant: evaluates infant neck position and head shape. Stroke in a Child or Adolescent: evaluates central focal weakness and seizures.
Transferable rule When a newborn will not move one arm, read three reflexes before the posture. A lower Moro alone with crepitus is a fracture. Lost Moro and biceps with a kept grasp is C5-C6. A lost grasp with Moro and biceps kept is C8-T1. With a lower-plexus injury, ptosis and miosis suggest T1 sympathetic involvement and a poorer outcome.
Upper and lower plexusThe classic C5-C6 pattern reduces Moro and biceps while preserving grasp. Lower-trunk injury instead weakens the hand and removes grasp.
Fracture comparisonClavicular crepitus with a pain-limited Moro and preserved grasp favors a fracture. An absent grasp instead supports the lower-trunk pattern.
Central weaknessUpper motor neuron signs favor a central lesion. A clawed hand with absent grasp and preserved upper reflexes supports lower-plexus localization.
Generalized weaknessAltered alertness and poor tone favor a generalized neonatal insult. Isolated hand weakness with absent grasp and preserved Moro and biceps favors the lower plexus.
